newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania students, pupils take up protest flame.
newsitem.headline: Albania students, pupils take up protest flame.

text.p: Albanian police used force against secondary school pupils on Friday, kicking and slapping them to prevent them joining university students protesting against a pyramid scheme scandal and the government.
Reporters saw some six plain-clothes police officers forcing a crowd of around 40 pupils aged between 16 and 18 to scatter as they walked towards Tirana university.
"It's outrageous," said one woman passer-by who saw male pupils being slapped across the face or kicked.
Around 3,000 schoolchildren attempted to gather in the city but police blocked streets and dispersed the groups moving across a park 500 metres (yards) from the presidency.
"Special forces...were kicking and punching us," said Edvin, aged 16.
"I said 'What are you doing? We are your sons, we are the sons of this country'," he said.
"Maybe tomorrow we will not be here. Maybe tomorrow we will be dead," another pupil said.
Rudina, 20, said: "They have punched us and treated us in a very bad way, but we are ready to protest to the end."
Police prevented Tirana students from beginning a hunger strike on Thursday. Two student leaders were bundled into cars and have not been seen since.
"They were both beaten. We have no news of them. They have disappeared," said 22-year-old student Emilio.
Uniformed police halted a crowd of younger pupils from the Partizani secondary school near central Skanderbeg Square from advancing too far out of their yard, but no force was used.

Students and pupils across the Balkan state have taken up the flame of anti-government protest after weeks of violent clashes between police and savers who lost heavily in fraudulent investment schemes.
Protesters have called for the resignation of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government, blaming ministers for failing to alert savers to the dangers of the pyramid schemes.

A sign of discord within the ruling right-wing Democratic Party was evident on Thursday when two senior Democrat deputies, Azem Hajdari and Bashkim Kopliku, told parliament that Meksi and his administration should quit.
A group of 12 Democrat dissident deputies have also spoken out against the Meksi government.
While the government is coming under pressure, Berisha appears unassailable. He will stand unopposed for re-election to a fresh five-year term in a parliamentary vote on Monday.

Berisha's main political rival, Socialist leader Fatos Nano, is in jail for corruption, though his supporters allege he is being held as a political prisoner. Smaller opposition parties have decided against challenging Berisha in the vote.
However the wave of protests is the most serious crisis facing Berisha and his Democrats since they came to power in 1992.
A group of 42 university students on hunger strike for the ninth day in the southern town of Vlore have become a beacon for student action across the country.
Thousands of people stage marches through the Adriatic port town daily against the government and in support of the students.
In Gjirokaster, 230 km (145 miles) south of Tirana, around 3,000 secondary school pupils gathered at the university on Friday to express solidarity with 43 students on hunger strike, witnesses said.
